title: What Do Models Still Suck At? - Peter Gostev, Arena.ai, BullshitBench
talk_summary: Peter Gostev presents BullshitBench, a 155-question benchmark of nonsense prompts showing many models (GPT, Gemini ~50/50) accept false premises instead of pushing back, with Claude models best and reasoning often making it worse. He also shows Arena's 'dissatisfaction rate' metric (both responses bad) which improved from ~17% to ~9% for top models, with uneven gains across expert categories like software, gaming, and law/finance.

takeaways.what_they_do: Feed models questions with impossible/contradictory premises and grade whether they refuse/reframe versus fabricate an answer, using an LLM judge validated by human reading.
takeaways.numbers: 155 questions; GPT/Gemini ~50/50 accept nonsense; Claude best

takeaways.what_they_do: Observed that reasoning models spend many paragraphs solving a task even after noting the premise is wrong; recommends training/behavior to sometimes not solve.
Speaker notes agents will happily execute a task aimed at the wrong project when many run in parallel.
Instead of only pairwise preference, track the fraction of cases where both candidate outputs are judged bad, giving a floor on quality rather than a relative ranking.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can also say when both models give a bad response ... Think of it as like dissatisfaction rate
takeaways.numbers: Top-25 models: ~17% pre-reasoning, ~12% after o1, ~9% now

takeaways.what_they_do: Break dissatisfaction down by task category (quantitative, software, gaming, law/finance) because aggregate gains hide flat categories.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the improvement is not really seen everywhere ... gaming is an interesting category

takeaways.technique: Don't crank reasoning for premise checks
takeaways.what_they_do: Found higher reasoning effort often did not help and sometimes hurt on nonsense-premise tasks.
takeaways.evidence_quote: reasoning often actually goes in reverse and doesn't help. It actually makes it worse
